title: Plastic Alternatives
desc: Understand materials that can replace single-use plastic, how to test them honestly, and how to plan a small product switch.
outcomes: Explain plastic types and the problem of waste.
Test an alternative for use and cost.
Judge claims such as biodegradable and compostable.
Plan a product switch for a small business.
task: Choose one single-use plastic item, test two alternatives, compare cost and impact, and write a switch plan with customer message.
condition: Samples of items, a scale and basic tools, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. Safe, non-food-contact tests unless approved.
standard: Tests are repeatable; claims are checked against recognised definitions; cost per use is shown; end-of-life route exists locally; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Shop owners, packaging buyers, students, municipal staff.
evidence: test sheet, comparison table, switch plan
modules: The plastic waste problem and your baseline
Understand
Single-use plastic is used for minutes and can last for centuries. Before you change anything, measure what you use.
Single-use items such as bags, bottles, sachets, cutlery and cups make up a large share of litter.
Microplastics from breakdown and from synthetic textiles enter water and food.
Order of action: reduce, reuse, recycle, and only then replace.
A switch that increases total impact is not an improvement.
A cafe counts 300 disposable cups a day. A returnable cup scheme with a deposit cuts that by 70 per cent, more than any new compostable cup could.
Audit the plastic you or your business use for one week: list items, counts and weight.
List has at least 15 items with counts, the top three are highlighted and a baseline weight is recorded.
Plastic types, codes and what is really recycled
Understand
Knowing the type tells you whether it can be recycled where you live.
Resin codes 1 to 7 show the polymer type.
PET (1) and HDPE (2) are widely collected; films, multilayer packs and black plastics are rarely recycled.
Dirty or mixed plastic is hard to sort.
Check what your local collectors actually accept.
PET bottles are often collected and recycled; a chips packet made of multilayer film usually goes to landfill. The municipal website lists only codes 1 and 2 for kerbside pickup.
Sort 10 items by code and local recyclability.
At least 9 sorted correctly and the local rule is cited.
Alternative materials and reuse systems
Understand
Many options exist and each has trade-offs. Reuse often beats replacement.
Paper and card, glass, metal, plant fibres, starch-based plastics and compostable blends.
Refill and returnable systems cut waste most.
Consider strength, moisture, heat, cost and local end-of-life facilities.
Ask suppliers for data, not slogans.

A bakery tests paper bags, starch bags and reusable cloth bags. Paper works but costs more; a cloth bag discount scheme halves bag use. A refill station for detergent cuts bottle purchases by 80 per cent.
Make an options table for one product with at least four options including a reuse option.
Each option has pros, cons, cost and end-of-life route.
Testing alternatives
Apply
Test under real conditions before you switch.
Tests: strength (load until failure), leak, heat, cold, shelf life and user trial.
Repeat each test three times.
Record failures with photos and cost per use.
Test with real users.
A paper cup with a thin lining leaks after 25 minutes with hot tea; a better-lined version lasts an hour. A starch bag tears at 3 kg while paper holds 5 kg.
Test two alternatives against your current item and record results.
Table has repeated results and a conclusion.
Life-cycle thinking
Analyse
Look at the whole life: raw material, making, transport, use and end of life.
A reusable item wins after enough uses.
Local conditions change results, for example electricity mix and recycling rates.
State your boundaries and sources.
Compare per use, not per piece.
A glass jar needs about 12 uses to beat a plastic tub in emissions; a thicker reusable cup needs about 20 uses.
Do a simple life-cycle comparison for two options and calculate break-even uses.
Method and sources stated and arithmetic correct.
Claims, labels and greenwashing
Evaluate
Avoid being misled by green claims.
Biodegradable and compostable are not the same thing.
Compostable may need an industrial facility that your area lacks.
Look for recognised standards and ask for test reports.
Treat words such as eco and natural with caution.
A bag labelled eco has no standard number. The buyer asks for a test report and finds it is not compostable in home conditions, so the option is dropped.
Review three labels and score their claims.
Each review lists the evidence needed.
Customers, cost and communication
Evaluate
A switch must work for customers and the business.
Cost per use, not per piece.
Deposit or discount schemes.
Explain simply and train staff.
Track complaints and returns.
A refill discount repays the container cost within 20 uses; eight of ten surveyed customers accept a 5 INR deposit on a cup.
Cost your switch for one month and survey ten customers.
Cost sheet and survey results are recorded.
Switch plan and pilot
Create
Plan, pilot and review.
Steps, dates, owners and measures.
Pilot in one store or one product line.
Set a numeric goal such as 50 per cent fewer single-use items in 90 days.
Report results and decide to scale.
Plastic bags fall by 70 per cent in one month with a returnable bag scheme; after 90 days the shop meets a 62 per cent reduction in all single-use items.
Present the plan with measures and a decision rule.
Measures are numeric and dates are set.
quiz: Order of waste actions?

Reduce, reuse, recycle. (Covered in module 1: The plastic waste problem and your baseline. To pass that module: List has at least 15 items with counts, the top three are highlighted and a baseline weight is recorded.)
Why microplastics matter?

They enter food and water. (Covered in module 1: The plastic waste problem and your baseline. To pass that module: List has at least 15 items with counts, the top three are highlighted and a baseline weight is recorded.)
Compostable equals biodegradable?
No. (Covered in module 6: Claims, labels and greenwashing. To pass that module: Each review lists the evidence needed.)
Name a test.
Strength, leak, heat or shelf life. (Covered in module 4: Testing alternatives. To pass that module: Table has repeated results and a conclusion.)
Life-cycle stages?
Material, making, transport, use, end of life. (Covered in module 5: Life-cycle thinking. To pass that module: Method and sources stated and arithmetic correct.)
Why cost per use?
Reuse items spread cost. (Covered in module 7: Customers, cost and communication. To pass that module: Cost sheet and survey results are recorded.)
Name a label risk.
Greenwashing. (Covered in module 6: Claims, labels and greenwashing. To pass that module: Each review lists the evidence needed.)
Best first step?

Reduce. (Covered in module 1: The plastic waste problem and your baseline. To pass that module: List has at least 15 items with counts, the top three are highlighted and a baseline weight is recorded.)
Why pilot?
Test small first. (Covered in module 8: Switch plan and pilot. To pass that module: Measures are numeric and dates are set.)
Why local end-of-life?
Facilities differ. (Covered in module 3: Alternative materials and reuse systems. To pass that module: Each option has pros, cons, cost and end-of-life route.)
rubric: Both alternatives tested for strength, cost and use, with results tabled
Results include lifecycle claims checked against a public source
Bans, recycling streams and labels for the place are written down
Rules checked on the authority's page, dated, and a disposal route found

local: Packaging, food-contact and waste rules differ by place.
